summary:
Same-sex conduct between adults is lawful in Madagascar only from age 21. Article 331 of the Penal Code treats same-sex acts involving a person under 21 as indecent assault, with a reported penalty band of five to ten years' imprisonment. The age of consent is unequal, so a trans visitor whose partner or counterparty is under 21 carries a criminal exposure that a heterosexual visitor does not.

In a 2020 case a 33-year-old woman was arrested for the statutory rape of a 19-year-old woman after the younger woman's mother filed a complaint; the mother was allegedly acting to cover an incest and rape accusation against the father. Religious leaders offered the younger woman conversion therapy during the proceedings.

Marriage is closed to same-sex couples. Article 2 of Law No. 2007-022 on Marriage and Matrimonial Regimes prohibits marriage between two persons of the same sex, whether before the Civil Registrar or under traditional ceremonies. Article 39 of the same law names gender identity as a cause for absolute nullity of marriage, a direct legal exposure for a trans visitor whose marriage could be attacked on that ground. Neither same-sex marriage nor a civil union is recognised; a guide updated 3 December 2023 records the absence of both.

Official policy runs against protection. At Madagascar's fourth universal periodic review in January 2025 the government received 235 recommendations and rejected those calling for action against anti-LGBT violence and hate speech and for equalising the age of consent. Six Malagasy organisations, including Queer Place, Divers' Unité and Madagascar LGBT+, responded that refusing to act is to endorse impunity and condone violence.

The social climate constrains visibility. A France 24 'Focus' report of August 2024 found that although homosexuality is not illegal, it is widely considered socially unacceptable, and that many LGBT people hide their sexuality to keep their jobs and live in peace, relying on their own networks and coded language. Public expression has been stopped outright: in early July 2021 the Malagasy government cancelled an LGBTQ party held at a bar in Antananarivo on the grounds of incitement to debauchery.

Violence against trans people is documented but thinly sourced in time. The 2011 US State Department Human Rights Report recorded societal discrimination and violence against the LGBT community, with public attitudes ranging from tacit acceptance to violent rejection, and identified transgender sex workers as frequent targets of verbal abuse, stone throwing and even murder. The most recent documented instance of violence against a trans person in this record is that 2011 finding; no later instance is documented. The same report covered the post-coup regime and unlawful killings, which bears on how far state protection can be expected to function.

Health care is addressed mainly through HIV policy. Act No. 2005-040 on the Fight against HIV/AIDS requires information, education and communication programmes adapted to the sexual orientation of the target groups, and Article 26 mandates special provisions protecting vulnerable groups, expressly including young people, sex workers, men who have sex with men and mobile populations, against HIV transmission. In practice care access is complicated by the conversion therapy offered to the young woman in the 2020 proceedings and by the violent rejection recorded in 2011.
tangentialFactors:
Madagascar sits within a wider regional movement: an international news service reported in July 2020 that roughly 22 of 53 African states had moved to decriminalise same-sex conduct, with Madagascar's position being legality above 21 rather than full equality. That comparison is a count of jurisdictions, not a measure of risk per visitor.

Data protection law gives some cover to sensitive information. Article 18 of Law No. 2014-038 on the Protection of Personal Data bars processing of sensitive data including data on health or sexual life, and Article 2 of Law No. 2017-045 on Credit Information Bureaus likewise treats sexual orientation as sensitive data.

Hostility directed at visibility extends beyond trans people. The 2011 US State Department report recorded that supporters of a same-sex couple were subjected to insults and death threats on social media, and that religious leaders publicly accused them of promising homosexuality.

An international travel guide updated 3 December 2023 characterises the legal framework as limited in progress compared with other countries, with LGBT people facing discrimination and a lack of civic rights. The assessment is a comparison, not a finding about enforcement.
localsOnly:
Family formation is restricted to heterosexual married couples. Article 33 of Law No. 2005-014 on Adoption states that full adoption is only permitted to heterosexual spouses, which closes adoption to LGBT residents as a class.

Residents who are open about their sexuality report having to conceal it to keep employment, and sustain their own networks and coded language to live and work in peace, according to the France 24 report of August 2024.

Six Malagasy organisations — Queer Place, Mifoha Olo Mazoto, Divers' Unité, Justice Égalitaire, Men Engage and Madagascar LGBT+ — issued a joint protest at the government's rejection of the UN recommendations in January 2025, stating that refusing to act is to endorse impunity and condone violence.

Resources for LGBTQI+ people in country are catalogued by Rights in Exile (AsyLex), which also documents case law, state-protection capacity and supporting organisations.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory contains no entry, visa or border-screening rules, no document or gender-marker requirements, and no information on facilities or identification checks. Whether a trans visitor's documents are examined or flagged on arrival is not sourced here.

No case law applying Article 39 of Law No. 2007-022, under which gender identity voids a marriage, is documented in this record, and no instance of Article 331 being used against trans-specific conduct is sourced. Both provisions are stated as written law; their application remains unresolved.

No denominator, per-capita figure or population-survey data on violence against trans people appears in the inventory, so the magnitude of that risk cannot be ranked against other jurisdictions. The only trans-specific violence finding is the 2011 report, and no later trans-specific incident is documented.

Legal gender recognition, name and marker change procedures, and trans-specific health care beyond HIV policy are not covered by any source here. Whether any of these exist under Malagasy law is unresolved.
